summary: This is the expanded version of the pets' speak method: instead of one fixed greeting, each pet checks its battery level and then its mood, returning a different sentence for each situation. The three subclasses override speak so a cat, a bird, and a dog each say the same set of ideas in their own voice.

lines.text: The base class holds the behaviour shared by every robot pet; the ellipsis stands for the attributes and methods written in the earlier exercises, which stay exactly as they were.
The feature being added lives entirely inside this one method, so the tests written for it only ever need to call speak.
Battery is checked before mood because a nearly flat robot should complain about power no matter how it feels; the order of these checks is itself a design decision worth testing.
A full battery gets its own celebratory line, which is a useful boundary case: 99 and 100 must produce different answers.
Once power is not an issue, mood decides the message; each mood is a separate branch and therefore deserves its own test.
The final return is the fallback that runs when no earlier condition matched, so an unknown mood still produces a sensible sentence rather than None.
Each subclass inherits everything from RobotPet and then replaces only what should sound different.
Defining speak again in the subclass overrides the parent version, so a RobotCat object always uses the cat wording even though the decision structure is identical.

lines.code: return f"{self.name} says: 'ARF ARF ARF! LET\'S PLAY!'"
lines.text: The backslash escapes the apostrophe in LET'S so it is treated as text rather than as the end of the single-quoted string.
